lead: Both readings today put a son in front of hostile power. Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God” and of Christ Jesus, who “made the good confession” before Pontius Pilate, and he ends with a hymn to the God who dwells in unapproachable light. In Luke, the owner of a vineyard sends servant after servant to his tenants, and last of all his beloved son, whom they throw out and kill. In this season the Church hears the parable knowing how the story ended: the Son who was rejected is risen. The key words are confession, appearing and heir.

set: The First Letter to Timothy closes with a solemn charge to a young leader of the church at Ephesus. The letter presents itself as Paul's; many scholars think it was written later in Paul's name by a disciple, while others hold that it is his own. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

Just before these verses Paul reminds Timothy of the confession he made “in the presence of many witnesses” (6:12), most likely at his baptism or his ordination. Now he sets that confession beside the confession of Christ himself.
str: v. 13: the charge, given before God the giver of life and before Christ the faithful witness.
v. 14: keep the commandment until the Lord appears.
vv. 15–16: a hymn to God, the only Sovereign, who alone has immortality.
kw: To say the same thing, to agree openly. It is used of Timothy's confession in v. 12 and of Christ's in v. 13. The Christian's word of faith echoes the word Christ spoke at his trial.
A shining forth. The Pastoral Letters prefer this word for the Lord's return, and they also use it for his first coming (2 Timothy 1:10).
Found only here in the New Testament. God is not far away by choice; his light is simply beyond what creatures can reach, unless he comes near to us.
vv: In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you
This is the only place in the letters of Paul where Pilate is named. The Creed keeps the same memory: “suffered under Pontius Pilate”. Our faith is tied to a real trial, on a real day.
It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
Many scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn the church already sang. The God no one can see has been made known in the Son (John 1:18).
ch: The Catechism recalls that before Pilate Christ declared that he came into the world “to bear witness to the truth”, and that the Christian is called not to be ashamed of testifying to the Lord (CCC 2471). Every confession of faith made at baptism, in the Creed of the Holy Qurbana, or before a hostile world shares in that first confession. The doxology of v. 16 has passed into Christian prayer: we adore a God who is beyond us, and we approach him only because he has approached us.

r.h: I will send my beloved son
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders have just asked him by what authority he acts (20:1–8). He answers with a parable told to the people, but aimed, as Luke says, at those leaders (20:19).

Every listener would have heard Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), where the vineyard is the house of Israel. Absentee landlords and quarrels with tenants were also a familiar part of life in Galilee.
str: v. 9: the vineyard planted and leased.
vv. 10–12: three servants, each treated worse.
v. 13: the owner's decision: “my beloved son”.
vv. 14–15a: the plot and the killing outside the vineyard.
vv. 15b–16: the owner's response, and the people's cry, “Heaven forbid!”
kw: The words of the Father's voice at the Jordan (Luke 3:22). The parable has its hearers understand who the last messenger is.
Only Luke has the owner say “perhaps they will respect him”. It is the hope of a father who keeps trying, even when the servants have been beaten.
The tenants think that by killing the heir they will gain the inheritance. In the Easter faith the opposite happens: the heir is raised and shares the inheritance with all who are his (Romans 8:17).
vv: I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.
The question “What shall I do?” is the question of a God who will not give up on his vineyard.
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.
Luke and Matthew put the throwing out before the killing. Hebrews remembers that Jesus suffered outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:12).
He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.
The vineyard is not destroyed; the unfaithful tenants are. The warning is to those entrusted with the care of God's people in every age, the shepherds of the Church included.
ch: The Fathers, St Irenaeus among them, read the servants as the prophets and the son as Christ (in substance). The Church reads the parable as a word about her Lord's Passion, and never as a charge against the Jewish people: Luke shows that the people hung on his words, and that the leaders of that day were the ones addressed (19:48; 20:19; CCC 597). In the Resurrection the rejected Son becomes, in the verse that follows the reading, the cornerstone (20:17; Psalm 118:22).

qa: Does “give the vineyard to others” mean that God has rejected Israel?

No. In Luke the parable is addressed to the leaders who rejected Jesus, and the people themselves cry out against the thought of such an ending. Paul teaches that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Church holds that the Jewish people remain beloved of God (CCC 839). The new tenants are the apostles and their successors, who will be judged by the same standard.
study: Where am I asked today to make “the good confession”, at work, at home or among friends?
The owner keeps sending, even after the servants are beaten. Where has God kept sending to me when I did not respond?
